title: Paper Plane packet v1.2 (DRAFT)
description: Tender/cargo split. A small tender carries the manifest and the offers; the bytes travel by whichever method the RECEIVER chooses. A tender may also name a hold: a place where the cargo waits, independent of the card that sent it, so the sender can go away. v1 delivery is same-host; the hold is what makes cross-host possible.

id.description: UUIDv4 from the sender. Idempotency key for the whole transfer.

from.description: Sender card id (routing only, never identity).

to.description: Recipient card id (routing only, never identity).

ttlSec.description: Tender/metadata shelf life. Default 259200 (72h), floor 172800 (48h). The cargo token may never outlive this.

capabilities.description: Enforced at receive time, before the payload is opened.

sha256.description: Hash of the bytes AS TRANSPORTED, i.e. ciphertext. A relay can verify it without holding the key, which is the point.

plaintextSha256.description: Optional. Hash of the bytes after decryption, so the receiver can prove the plaintext is intact. Never trusted by the relay.

offers.description: Ordered by sender preference. The RECEIVER picks exactly one; it is the only party that knows its free space and whether a guest is running.

endpoint.description: guest-fetch / pull-http only. Loopback or relay URL.

value.description: Opaque capability token. Never a bearer secret in a URL that can be logged unhashed.

chosen.description: Set by the receiver in its reply. Absent until the receiver answers.

keyWrap.description: Required whenever cipher is set. The content key, wrapped for the recipient only. Without this a relay can read every plane it holds, which makes 'encrypted' decorative.

senderEphemeralPublicKey.description: Per-transfer X25519 public key. Never reused.

wrappedKey.description: Content key encrypted under the ECDH-derived KEK.

hold.description: Optional. Where the cargo waits so the sender's card can close. A hold is not a delivery method and not an inbox: it is staging with a lease. Ownership stays with the sender until the receiver fetches.

kind.description: host = this machine's data dir, card-independent. relay = a provider (Supabase). Only relay survives the sender's machine going away.

state.description: staged = upload in flight, not yet trusted. held = complete, hash-verified, pending pickup. leased = a client has claimed it and the visibility lease is running. released = the receiver ACKed; the sender now holds a receipt. failed = retries exhausted. expired = past deadline, awaiting purge. purged = bytes confirmed gone.

holdExpiresAt.description: Replaces the old senderAvailableUntil idea: availability is a property of the hold, not of the sender being awake. Never later than tender.createdAt + ttlSec.

ref.description: Opaque locator. Useless without a token; safe to log.

maxFetchBytes.description: Transport ceiling for one fetch, if the provider caps file size. A hold that exceeds it is refused at stage time, never half-delivered.

tenderId.description: The tender that authorised this cargo.

value.description: Recipient signature over sha256(payload) + plane id.

x-token-policy.rule: token.expiresAt <= tender.createdAt + ttlSec. A token may never outlive the tender that issued it.
x-token-policy.floorIsCapNotFloor: The 48h minimum is a preferred duration, not a guarantee: a tender with ttlSec under 48h cannot issue a 48h token. Compute token.expiresAt = min(issuedAt + 48h, tender.expiresAt). Do not reject a short tender because it cannot reach the floor.
x-token-policy.longTransfers: If a transfer can outlive the token, the receiver asks for a fresh token before expiry and the old one is burned. Rotation is per-chunk-batch, not per-byte.
x-token-policy.enforcement: Server-side only. A hidden client button is not expiry.
x-token-policy.onExpiry: Purge the cargo bytes, not just the index row. Expired means gone from disk.
x-token-policy.clockSkew: Allow 120s skew. Reject anything beyond that.
x-token-policy.replay: One-time: consume the token on first successful open, then burn it even if the hash check fails.
x-token-policy.neverASignedUrl: The plane token is never a provider signed URL. Signed URLs generally cannot be revoked individually, so shelf life and burn-on-failure cannot be enforced through them. Validate the token first, then mint a transport URL with a 60-300s life.
x-token-policy.atRest: Store a hash of the token, never the token. A table dump must not be replayable.

x-relay.why: A held cargo outlives the card because the bytes sit with a provider, not on a card. This is the only thing that makes a sender closing their laptop harmless.

mapping.cargo: storage bucket 'plane-holds', object path keyed by plane id

x-relay.keyedBy: plane id, never card id. Deleting a card must never destroy a held plane.
x-relay.confidentiality: The relay stores ciphertext only. It never holds a content key, so a provider breach leaks chunk sizes and timing, not planes. The recipient key arrives as tender.keyWrap; without it the hold is not end-to-end encrypted and must not be described as such.
x-relay.hashScope: manifest.sha256 covers the transported (encrypted) bytes, so the relay can verify integrity without a key. plaintextSha256 is the receiver's own post-decrypt check.
x-relay.expiry: mark_expired_holds() marks; a janitor purges through the Storage API. Deleting the storage row directly orphans the file and keeps billing it.
x-relay.limitsAsOf: 2026-11-18, free plan: 50 MiB per file, 1 GB total, project paused after ~7 days idle. Pro: 500 GB per file, 100 GB included, never paused.
x-relay.honesty: A free-tier relay is fine for tenders and for files up to 50 MiB. It cannot carry a guest. Do not advertise guest transfer over a relay until the plan and the upload path both exist.

x-landing-events.landed: Transport: bytes are on the receiver's side, fsynced, hash-verified. The sender is allowed to know this.
x-landing-events.taken: Receiver: the guest, an app, or the user did something with it. The sender does NOT get to know this unless the receiver chooses to sign a receipt.

x-store-and-forward.why: The only delivery model where neither end has to be awake at the same time. The sender writes once and is done; the receiver converges whenever it next connects. Everything else in this contract is an optimisation on top of it.

roles.mailbox: The database. Holds every sent plane until it is ACKed, plus history after.
roles.client: A PC. Pulls, writes locally, fsyncs, then ACKs.

states.held: pending — fetchable, nobody has claimed it
states.leased: claimed by a client, visibility lease running

x-store-and-forward.ackOrder: Write locally, fsync, then ACK. Never the reverse. ACK-then-crash loses the plane; write-then-crash only duplicates it, and the receiver dedupes on plane id.
x-store-and-forward.ordering: A server-side monotonic sequence, never a timestamp. Timestamps collide within a millisecond, jump on clock steps, and cannot be a cursor.
x-store-and-forward.recovery: An expired lease makes a row eligible again. A client that dies mid-fetch strands nothing and cleans up nothing.
x-store-and-forward.retention: Delivered rows keep metadata so history stays readable; bytes purge after the retention window. On a 1 GB store, 'never delete' is a wish.
x-store-and-forward.pushIsOptional: Polling is the baseline and must converge on its own. WebSocket or LISTEN/NOTIFY only lowers latency; it is never required for correctness.

x-not-in-v1: Deriving key material from card ids. Card ids are public and are never keys.
Binding trust to a card id. Remote identity belongs to a person: person key -> device key -> ephemeral per-transfer key.
Silent TOFU for remote senders. First contact needs a visible fingerprint.
Implying peer-to-peer across machines while delivery is same-host only.
Relaying guest-sized cargo over the free plan. 12 GiB against a 50 MiB file cap is not a tuning problem.
Treating 'delivered' as 'read'. Delivery is an ACK that the bytes arrived and were written; whether a human opened them is a separate fact the sender has no right to.
Deleting a plane on ACK. The bytes may go after the retention window; the record stays, or history and receipts die with it.
